q: In neutral organic molecules, how many covalent bonds do C, N, O and Cl usually form, in that order?
h: Count the valence electrons each atom needs to reach an octet; each bond supplies one electron.
w: C needs 4 more electrons, N needs 3, O needs 2 and Cl needs 1, so the usual bond counts are 4, 3, 2, 1. Hydrogen also forms just one bond.
x: This swaps N and O. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more for an octet, while oxygen has 6 and needs only 2.
Chlorine has 7 valence electrons, so it needs just one more electron to reach an octet. That means one bond, like hydrogen.
This swaps C and O. Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more, while oxygen needs only 2.

q: What is the approximate H–C–H bond angle in ethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Each carbon has four single bonds (four electron groups). Which shape spreads four groups as far apart as possible?
w: Four bonded groups around carbon give a tetrahedral shape with angles of about 109.5°. 120° goes with a C=C double bond and 180° with a triple bond.
x: 120° goes with a carbon that has three electron groups, like a C=C carbon. Each carbon in ethane has four single bonds.
180° is the linear angle for two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Ethane's carbons have four groups each.
90° angles would crowd four groups together. Four groups spread out in 3-D, not in a flat square.

q: What is the shape around each carbon atom in ethene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>?
h: A double bond counts as one electron group. How many groups surround each carbon?
w: Each carbon has three groups (two H and the double bond to the other C), so it is trigonal planar with ~120° angles. Tetrahedral is for carbons with four single bonds.
x: Tetrahedral goes with four electron groups, like a carbon with four single bonds. In ethene the double bond counts as one group.
Linear goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around each ethene carbon.
Bent, about 105°, describes an atom like the O in water, with two bonds and two lone pairs. Carbon in ethene has no lone pairs.

q: Which of these molecules is polar?
h: Look for an electronegative atom (F, N, O) whose bond dipole is not canceled by symmetry.
w: Methanol's polar O–H and C–O bonds do not cancel, so CH3OH is polar. CCl4 and CO2 have polar bonds arranged symmetrically, so their dipoles cancel; propane has only nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds.
x: CCl<sub>4</sub> has polar C–Cl bonds, but they point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.
Propane has only C–C and C–H bonds, which are essentially nonpolar, so the molecule is nonpolar.
CO<sub>2</sub> has polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

q: Compared with sodium chloride, the organic compound hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>, would be expected to
c: melt at a much lower temperature
h: Think about covalent molecules held together by weak attractions versus an ionic lattice.
w: Hexane is a nonpolar covalent compound with weak attractions between molecules, so it melts at a much lower temperature than ionic NaCl. It has no ions to conduct and is insoluble in water.
x: Conducting when melted needs ions that can move. Hexane is a covalent molecule with no ions.
Hexane is nonpolar, with only C–C and C–H bonds, so it does not mix with polar water. "Like dissolves like."
Hexane contains only covalent C–C and C–H bonds. Ionic bonds hold compounds like NaCl together.

q: Which functional group is present in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Where is the oxygen? Is it bonded to H, to a C=O, or between two carbon groups?
w: An oxygen bonded to two carbon groups, R–O–R, is an ether (this one is diethyl ether, an old anesthetic). An alcohol needs an –OH group.
x: An alcohol has an –OH group. In this compound the oxygen has no H; it sits between two carbon groups.
That group needs a C=O next to the oxygen (–COO–). This molecule has no C=O at all.
A ketone has a C=O bonded to two carbons. This molecule has no double bond to oxygen.

q: Which functional group is present in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Write out –COO–: is the second oxygen bonded to H or to a carbon?
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to an –O–CH3 group, so it is an ester (methyl propanoate). A carboxylic acid would be –COOH, with H on the oxygen.
x: A carboxylic acid is –COOH, with H on the second oxygen. Here that oxygen is bonded to a CH<sub>3</sub> instead.
That group has an O between two carbons with no C=O next to it. Here one of the carbons on the O is a C=O carbon.
An aldehyde has a C=O at the end of a chain bonded to H (–CHO). Here the C=O carbon is bonded to another oxygen.

q: The compound CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> contains which functional group?
h: Is the nitrogen attached directly to a carbonyl (C=O) carbon?
w: The –NH2 is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes an amide (ethanamide). An amine has nitrogen bonded only to carbons or H, with no C=O next to it.
x: In an amine, N is bonded only to carbons or H with no C=O next to it. Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on a C=O carbon.
A ketone has a C=O bonded to two carbons. Here the C=O carbon is bonded to a nitrogen.
That group has –COO–, an oxygen on the C=O carbon. Here the C=O carbon carries an –NH<sub>2</sub> instead.

q: Which condensed formula is NOT a possible structure?
h: Count the bonds on every carbon. Carbon must have exactly four.
w: In CH3CH2=CH2 the middle carbon has a bond to CH3, two H atoms and a double bond, which is 5 bonds, so it is impossible. In CH3CH=CH2 the middle carbon has 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 bonds.
x: This one is fine: the middle carbon has a bond to CH<sub>3</sub>, one H and a double bond, for 4 bonds. Look for a carbon with 5.
This is ethanol, a real compound. Every carbon has four bonds and O has two. Check the other formulas carbon by carbon.
This is propyne, a real compound. The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has 4 bonds, and each triple-bonded carbon has 3 + 1 = 4.

q: In a skeletal (line-angle) formula, each corner and each line end represents
c: a carbon atom plus enough H atoms for four bonds
a hydrogen atom bonded to a carbon atom
a carbon atom with no hydrogen atoms attached
an oxygen or nitrogen atom with its H atoms
h: Skeletal formulas leave out some atoms to save time. Which atoms are not drawn?
w: Corners and ends are carbon atoms; the H atoms on carbon are not drawn but are understood to fill each carbon to four bonds. Heteroatoms such as O and N are always written in.
x: Hydrogen atoms on carbon are the ones left out of a skeletal formula, not shown by corners. Each corner stands for a heavier atom.
Corners and ends do carry hydrogens; they are just not drawn. You add enough H to give each of those atoms four bonds.
O and N are always written out in a skeletal formula. Unlabeled corners and ends stand for a different element.

q: What is the molecular formula of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH?
h: Count every C, every H (including the one on oxygen) and every O.
w: C: 3. H: 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8. O: 1. The formula is C3H8O. Forgetting the H on the –OH gives the C3H7O distractor.
x: This misses the H on the –OH. Count every H, including the one on oxygen.
This has two H too few, which would need a C=O or C=C. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH has only single bonds.
Count the carbons again: CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub> are three carbon groups.

q: Which bond is the most polar?
h: Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms.
w: O (3.5) and H (2.1) differ by 1.4, more than N–H (0.9) or C–H (0.4); C–C is nonpolar. So O–H is the most polar.
x: N–H is polar, but N (3.0) and H (2.1) differ by only 0.9. Look for a bigger electronegativity difference.
C (2.5) and H (2.1) differ by only 0.4, so C–H is nearly nonpolar.
Two identical atoms share electrons equally, so C–C is nonpolar.

q: What is the shape around the nitrogen atom in trimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N?
h: Count the electron groups on N, including its lone pair, then name the shape from the bonded atoms only.
w: N has three bonded C atoms and one lone pair: four electron groups, but only three are atoms, so the shape is trigonal pyramidal (like NH3). Trigonal planar would need no lone pair.
x: Trigonal planar needs three groups and no lone pair. The N in an amine still has a lone pair, which pushes the bonds down.
Four electron groups are arranged tetrahedrally, but the shape is named from atoms only. N here has three atoms and a lone pair.
Bent is for two bonded atoms plus lone pairs, like water. This N has three bonded carbons.

q: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH?
h: The carboxylic acid outranks the alcohol: it sets the suffix and its carbon is C1. Count all four carbons.
w: The –COOH carbon is C1 of a 4-carbon chain, and the –OH is on C4 as a hydroxy prefix: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid. 3-Hydroxypropanoic acid forgets that the COOH carbon is part of the chain.
x: The –COOH carbon is C1, and its OH is part of the acid group. The extra –OH is on the far end of the chain.
The -al ending is for an aldehyde, –CHO. This compound has a –COOH group, which takes the -oic acid ending.
This counts only 3 chain carbons. The –COOH carbon is part of the chain, so count it too.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH?
h: The ketone outranks the alcohol, so it gets the suffix and the lower number.
w: Number from the end nearest the C=O: ketone on C2, –OH on C4: 4-hydroxy-2-butanone. 1-Hydroxy-3-butanone gives the ketone the higher number, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone is a different compound, CH3COCH(OH)CH3.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. The ketone outranks the alcohol, so number to give the C=O carbon the lowest number.
The -al ending is for an aldehyde, with C=O at the end of the chain. Here the C=O is in the middle, between two carbons.
3-Hydroxy would put the –OH on the carbon next to the C=O, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. Here the –OH is on the end CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: The longest chain may run into the group written in parentheses. Count every path from end to end.
w: Going from the propyl group through the CH to an ethyl group gives a 6-carbon chain with an ethyl branch on C3: 3-ethylhexane. 3-Propylpentane uses a shorter 5-carbon chain; 4-ethylhexane numbers from the wrong end. 3-Methylheptane is a different isomer of C8H18.
x: Pentane is not the longest chain. Follow a path that runs from the propyl group, through the CH, into one ethyl group.
This numbers from the wrong end. Number the chain so the branch gets the lowest possible number.
A 7-carbon chain is not possible here; the longest path is shorter. 3-Methylheptane is a different isomer of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>.

q: Vanillin, the flavor of vanilla, is a benzene ring bearing –OH, –OCH<sub>3</sub> and –CHO groups. Which functional groups does it contain?
h: –OH on a benzene ring has a special name. An O between two carbons with no C=O is ... ? –CHO is ... ?
w: –OH bonded directly to a benzene ring = phenol; Ar–O–CH3 (no C=O next to the O) = ether; –CHO = aldehyde: phenol, ether, aldehyde. An ester needs –COO–.
x: –OH on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol. An ester needs a C=O next to the O, and –CHO (C=O with H) is not a ketone.
An ester needs –COO–, a C=O next to the oxygen. The –OCH<sub>3</sub> here has no C=O beside it.
–OH directly on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol. And –CHO has no –OH, so it is not a carboxylic acid.

q: A skeletal (line-angle) formula is a zigzag of four line segments with a double line for the first segment and no other atoms shown. What is its molecular formula?
h: Four segments have five ends/corners, each a carbon. Fill in H so each carbon has four bonds.
w: Four segments connect 5 carbons: CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3. Adding H to give each C four bonds: 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10 H, so C5H10. Counting segments instead of carbons gives C4; ignoring the double line gives C5H12.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> ignores the double line. A C=C double bond means two fewer H than an alkane.
This counts segments instead of carbons. Each end and each corner is a carbon, and four segments have five of these.
C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> would need two double bonds or a triple bond. There is only one double line here.

q: Count the atoms in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>. Which molecular formula is correct?
h: Count each group: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> counts twice. The COO has no H.
w: C: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6. H: 6 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 12. O: 2. Formula = C6H12O2. C6H14O2 is what you get by assuming every compound has 2n + 2 H; the ester C=O removes two.
x: That is the alkane formula, 2n + 2 H. The C=O in the ester group removes two H.
This is one carbon short. Remember (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> means two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the –OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon counts too.
This is one H short. Recount: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives 6 H, then CH, CH<sub>2</sub> and OCH<sub>3</sub>.

q: In propyne, CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH, what angle is formed by the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon and the two triple-bonded carbons?
h: Count the electron groups around a triple-bonded carbon. Two groups → which geometry?
w: Each triple-bonded carbon has only two electron groups (the triple bond counts as one), so it is linear: 180°. 109.5° applies to the CH3 carbon, and 120° to C=C carbons.
x: 120° goes with a carbon that has three electron groups, like a C=C carbon. A triple-bonded carbon has fewer groups.
109.5° is the angle around the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon, which has four single bonds. The question asks about the angle at a triple-bonded carbon.
90° angles are not found around carbon in this course. Count the electron groups on the middle carbon; the triple bond counts as one.

q: Lidocaine, a local anesthetic used in dentistry, is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>3</sub>–NH–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–N(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Which two nitrogen-containing groups does it have?
h: Is each N bonded to a C=O carbon? If not, count the carbons on that N.
w: The –NH– is bonded to a C=O carbon, so it is an amide (not a 2° amine). The other N carries three carbons (CH2 and two ethyls) with no C=O: a 3° amine. There is no –COO–, so no ester.
x: The –NH– is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes it an amide, not an amine. Then count carbons on the other N.
An ester needs –COO–, a C=O next to an oxygen. The C=O here is bonded to nitrogen.
There is no –NH<sub>2</sub>, so no 1° amine. The C=O carbon is bonded to N, so it is not a ketone either.

q: Eugenol, shown, is the main component of clove oil and is used in dentistry in temporary fillings and as a mild pain reliever. Which functional groups does eugenol contain?
h: Look at each oxygen: is it bonded to H, or between two carbons, and is there any C=O? Then look at the side chain.
w: The –OH on the benzene ring is a phenol; the –O– between the ring and CH3 is an ether (no C=O, so not an ester); the side chain has a C=C, an alkene. There is no C=O anywhere, so ketone and ester are wrong, and there is no triple bond.
x: An ester needs a C=O next to the oxygen. Eugenol has no C=O; the –O– between the ring and CH<sub>3</sub> has only single bonds.
–OH on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol, and the side chain has a C=C double bond, not a triple bond.
A ketone needs a C=O. Look again: none of eugenol's oxygens is double-bonded to carbon.

q: Lidocaine, shown, is a local anesthetic that dentists inject before filling a tooth. Which functional groups does it contain (besides the benzene ring)?
c: an amide and a tertiary (3°) amine
an ester and a tertiary (3°) amine
an amide and a primary (1°) amine
a ketone and a secondary (2°) amine
h: A C=O bonded directly to N is one group. For the other N, count the carbons attached to it.
w: The C=O is bonded to N–H, so that part is an amide (not a ketone, and not an ester since there is no –O–). The other N is bonded to three carbons (two ethyl groups and a CH2), so it is a tertiary amine. (Older anesthetics like procaine are esters.)
x: An ester needs a C=O next to an oxygen (–COO–). In lidocaine the C=O is bonded to a nitrogen, and there is no –O– at all.
A primary amine has –NH<sub>2</sub>, with only one carbon on N. Count the carbons on the N that is not next to the C=O.
A ketone needs a C=O between two carbons, but here the C=O is bonded to N. And an N–H next to a C=O is not an amine.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Number the main chain from the OH end. Which carbon carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: The chain is HO–C1–C2–C3–C4 with the CH3 branch on C2 (the CH right next to the CH2OH): 2-methyl-1-butanol, C5H12O. The most tempting wrong drawing moves the branch one carbon away from the OH (3-methyl-1-butanol); another puts the OH on the branched carbon; the 4-carbon one has dropped a CH2.
x: This drawing has only four carbons (2-methyl-1-propanol). The condensed formula has five carbons; one CH<sub>2</sub> is missing.
Here the branch is two carbons away from the C–OH carbon (3-methyl-1-butanol). In the formula, the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) sits right next to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
Here the –OH is on the branched carbon, which also holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups (2-methyl-2-butanol). In the formula the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub> at the end.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Count the carbons (every line end and corner is a C), then find which two carbons share the double bond.
w: Five carbons with the C=C between C2 and C3: 2-pentene. Putting the double bond at the end of the chain gives 1-pentene, a common slip when a drawing starts the zig-zag at the double bond. 2-Butene is one carbon short, and 2-methyl-2-butene has a branch the formula does not show.
x: Here the double bond is at the end of the chain (1-pentene). The formula starts with CH<sub>3</sub>, so the C=C begins at the second carbon.
This drawing has only four carbons (2-butene). Count the carbons in the formula again.
This drawing has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on a double-bond carbon (2-methyl-2-butene). The formula is an unbranched chain.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– means a carbon holding two methyl groups. Count the longest chain and locate the branch.
w: The longest chain is five carbons with one CH3 on C2: 2-methylpentane. The drawing with the branch on the middle carbon is 3-methylpentane (branch moved), the 2-methylbutane drawing is one CH2 short, and the one with two methyls on C2 has an extra carbon.
x: Here the branch is on the middle carbon of a five-carbon chain (3-methylpentane). (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– puts the branch one carbon from the end.
This drawing has only five carbons in all (2-methylbutane). The formula has six; one CH<sub>2</sub> is missing.
Here one carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> branches, for seven carbons. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– means a CH holding two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, one of which is part of the main chain.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: A C=O in the middle of a chain written as "CO" is a ketone. Which carbon holds the oxygen?
w: CO sits with two CH2CH3 groups on either side, so the C=O is on C3 of a five-carbon chain: 3-pentanone. 2-Pentanone moves the C=O one carbon over; butanone is one carbon short; pentanal puts the C=O at the end (an aldehyde, written CHO).
x: Here the C=O is on the second carbon (2-pentanone). In the formula, CO has a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on each side.
This drawing has only four carbons (butanone). Count the carbons on both sides of the CO again.
Here the C=O is at the end of the chain, an aldehyde (pentanal). In the formula the CO is in the middle, between two carbons.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Write the main chain left to right: C1 has the OH-bearing neighbor; the last CH holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
w: C1 = CH3, C2 = CH(OH), C3 = CH2, C4 = CH with a CH3 branch, and C5 is the other CH3: 4-methyl-2-pentanol. The tempting near-miss puts the methyl branch on C3, right beside the OH carbon (3-methyl-2-pentanol). Another moves the OH to the end of the chain, and 3-methyl-2-butanol is one CH2 short.
x: Here the –OH is on the end carbon of the chain (4-methyl-1-pentanol). In the formula the OH is on the CH next to the first CH<sub>3</sub>.
Here the CH<sub>3</sub> branch is right beside the C–OH carbon (3-methyl-2-pentanol). In the formula a CH<sub>2</sub> separates them.
This drawing has only five carbons (3-methyl-2-butanol). The CH<sub>2</sub> between the C–OH carbon and the branched CH is missing.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: An O written between two carbon groups is an ether oxygen. Count the carbons on each side of it.
w: Two carbons on one side of the O and three on the other: ethyl propyl ether. Moving the O so it has one carbon on one side gives methyl butyl ether (same formula, wrong structure); diethyl ether has only four carbons; 1-pentanol has an OH at the end, not an O between carbons.
x: Here the O has one carbon on one side and four on the other (methyl butyl ether). The formula has two carbons on one side and three on the other.
This drawing has only four carbons, two on each side of the O. Count the carbons on each side in the formula again.
This has an –OH at the end of a chain, an alcohol. In the formula the O sits between two carbon groups and has no H.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: In COOCH<sub>3</sub>, the C=O carbon is attached to the chain on its left; the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the single-bonded O.
w: Three carbons + the C=O carbon make a four-carbon acid part, and CH3 sits on the –O–: methyl butanoate. Ethyl propanoate has the same formula but the carbons are split 3 + 2 around the ester O; methyl propanoate is one carbon short; propyl acetate reverses which side carries the C=O.
x: Here the carbons are split 3 on the C=O side and 2 on the O side (ethyl propanoate). The formula has CH<sub>3</sub> alone on the single-bonded O.
This drawing has only four carbons (methyl propanoate). Count the carbons before the COO again: three plus the C=O carbon.
Here the C=O is on the short side and the long chain is on the –O– (propyl acetate). In the formula the long chain is attached to the C=O carbon.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Start at the CH<sub>2</sub>= end: the double bond is C1=C2. Which carbon carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: C1=C2 double bond, then C3 holds the CH3 branch, then an ethyl end: 3-methyl-1-pentene. The drawing with the double bond inside the chain (3-methyl-2-pentene) moved the C=C; the 4-methyl one moved the branch; 3-methyl-1-butene is one carbon short.
x: Here the double bond is inside the chain (3-methyl-2-pentene). CH<sub>2</sub>= at the start of the formula puts the C=C at the very end.
Here the branch is two carbons from the C=C (4-methyl-1-pentene). In the formula the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) comes right after CH<sub>2</sub>=CH.
This drawing has only five carbons (3-methyl-1-butene). The formula ends with a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, not just a CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: HC≡C– puts the triple bond at the very end of the chain. Then count to the carbon with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
w: C1≡C2, a CH2, then a CH bearing two CH3 groups: 4-methyl-1-pentyne. Moving the triple bond inside the chain gives 4-methyl-2-pentyne (no CH2 left between); 3-methyl-1-butyne lacks the CH2; 3-methyl-1-pentyne moves the branch next to the triple bond.
x: Here the triple bond is inside the chain (4-methyl-2-pentyne). HC≡C– at the start of the formula puts it at the very end.
This drawing has no CH<sub>2</sub> between the triple bond and the branched CH (3-methyl-1-butyne). The formula has one.
Here the branch is right next to the triple bond, followed by an ethyl end (3-methyl-1-pentyne). In the formula a CH<sub>2</sub> comes first, then a CH with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: The NH<sub>2</sub> in parentheses is attached to the CH written just before it.
w: The NH2 is on the second carbon from the right end of a five-carbon chain: 2-pentanamine. 3-Pentanamine moves the NH2 to the middle carbon; 1-pentanamine puts it at the end; 2-butanamine is one CH2 short.
x: Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on the end carbon (1-pentanamine). In the formula the NH<sub>2</sub> is on a CH, not a CH<sub>2</sub>.
Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on the middle carbon (3-pentanamine). In the formula the CH(NH<sub>2</sub>) has a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side.
This drawing has only four carbons (2-butanamine). Count the CH<sub>2</sub> groups in the formula again.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Find the carbon bonded to the O. Is it at the end of the chain or inside it?
w: The O–H hangs from the second carbon of a four-carbon chain, so that carbon is written CH(OH): CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (2-butanol). Writing CH2OH at the end would move the OH to C1; an O between two carbons would be an ether.
x: This puts the –OH on the end carbon (1-butanol). In the drawing the O is attached to a carbon inside the chain that has only one H.
This has an O between two carbons, an ether. In the drawing the O is bonded to H, so it is an –OH group.
This is a branched chain with the OH on a CH<sub>2</sub>. The drawing is an unbranched four-carbon chain.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: The end carbon has a C=O and one H. How is that group written in condensed form?
w: An end carbon with =O and one H is an aldehyde group, written CHO: CH3CH2CHO (propanal). CH3COCH3 would put the C=O in the middle (a ketone). Reading CHO as "C–O–H" leads students to the alcohol, but the drawing has no O–H bond.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> has its C=O in the middle of the chain, a ketone. In the drawing the C=O carbon is at the end and carries an H.
This is an alcohol with an O–H. The drawing has no O–H bond; the end carbon has a double bond to O and one H.
This has a C=C and an –OH. The drawing has no C=C and no O–H; the double bond is between C and O.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: A C=O carbon also bonded to an –O–C is an ester. Which side of the ester O does each carbon sit on?
w: CH3 on the C=O carbon, then –O–CH3: CH3COOCH3 (methyl acetate). Propanoic acid and ethyl formate have the same formula (C3H6O2) but different connections; the drawing has no O–H, so it is not an acid.
x: This is a carboxylic acid, with an O–H. The drawing has no O–H; the second O is bonded to a CH<sub>3</sub>.
Here the C=O carbon carries an H and the O carries an ethyl group. In the drawing the C=O carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub>, and the O carries a CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Count the carbons and note which one has three carbon neighbors.
w: The middle carbon is bonded to three CH3 groups and one H: CH3CH(CH3)CH3 (2-methylpropane, isobutane). The branch drawn downward is still a CH3 attached to the middle carbon, so the straight-chain butane formula is wrong; the other two have five carbons.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: The N sits inside the chain and carries one H. How many carbons are on each side of it?
w: One carbon on the left of N, two on the right, and one H on N: CH3NHCH2CH3 (ethylmethylamine, a 2° amine). Propylamine and trimethylamine have the same formula, C3H9N, but N–H counts of two and zero; diethylamine has four carbons.
x: This is propylamine, with N at the end bearing two H. In the drawing the N sits between two carbon groups and has one H.
Trimethylamine has three CH<sub>3</sub> groups on N and no N–H. The drawing has an N–H and an ethyl group.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Locate the C=C first, then the carbon with the CH<sub>3</sub> branch. Start writing from the CH<sub>2</sub>= end.
w: The C=C is at the end (CH2=CH–), and the next carbon is a CH bearing two CH3 groups: CH2=CHCH(CH3)2 (3-methyl-1-butene). CH3CH=C(CH3)2 moves the double bond to the branched carbon; the other two choices move the branch or remove it.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: The O in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is written between two carbon groups. Is it bonded to an H?

x: This drawing has an O–H on the end carbon, an alcohol (1-propanol). In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> the O has carbons on both sides and no H.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: CHO at the end of a formula is not C–O–H. Which group has a C=O plus an H on the same carbon?
w: CHO is the aldehyde group: the end carbon has a double bond to O and one H, giving acetaldehyde (ethanal). Reading CHO as C–O–H gives an alcohol, but ethanol has two more H atoms (C2H6O). The acid has an extra O, and dimethyl ether has no C=O.
x: This drawing is ethanol, with C–O–H. CHO means a C=O with an H on the same carbon, and there is no O–H.
This drawing has both a C=O and an O–H on the end carbon, a carboxylic acid. CHO has only one O.
This drawing has an O between two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, an ether. CHO means the O is double-bonded to the end carbon.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: In CONH<sub>2</sub>, the C has a double bond to O and a single bond to the NH<sub>2</sub>.
w: CH3–C(=O)–NH2: the carbonyl carbon is bonded to both O and N, which makes acetamide, an amide. N-Methylformamide (CH3NHCHO) and aminoacetaldehyde have the same formula but the C=O is not where the condensed formula puts it; ethylamine has no O.
x: Here the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the N, and the C=O carbon carries an H. In CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the C=O carbon.
This drawing has no oxygen at all (ethylamine). The CO in the formula is a C=O.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: COOH at the end of a formula is a carboxyl group: one C with =O and –OH.
w: The last carbon has =O and –OH, so the drawing is propanoic acid. Methyl acetate and ethyl formate are esters with the same formula, C3H6O2: they have an O between two carbons and no O–H. The hydroxy ketone moves the C=O into the chain.
x: This drawing has an O between the C=O carbon and a CH<sub>3</sub>, and no O–H. COOH needs an –OH on the C=O carbon.
This drawing has an H on the C=O carbon and an ethyl group on the other O, with no O–H. COOH needs an –OH on the C=O carbon.
Here the C=O is inside the chain and the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub>. In COOH both oxygens are on the same end carbon.

q: In this line structure of 1-butene, every corner is drawn at 120°. What is the actual C–C–C bond angle at carbon a, approximately?
h: Count the groups around carbon a, including the hydrogens the line drawing does not show. Does it have a double bond?
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (two C and two hidden H), so its groups point to the corners of a tetrahedron: about 109.5°. The zig-zag drawing makes every corner look like 120°, but only the two C=C carbons are really 120°.
x: 120° is the drawn angle, and it is real only at the two C=C carbons. Carbon a has only single bonds.
180° goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around carbon a, including hidden H.
90° is not the angle for any carbon in this molecule. Count the groups around carbon a, including the two hidden H.

q: Butanone (methyl ethyl ketone) is a common solvent. What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at carbon a?
h: Count the groups of electrons around carbon a. A double bond counts as one group.
w: Carbon a has three groups (two C and the C=O), which spread out in a flat triangle: about 120°. 109.5° applies to a carbon with four single bonds; the C=O counts as only one group.
x: 109.5° goes with a carbon that has four single bonds. Carbon a has a C=O, which counts as one group.
180° goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around carbon a.
90° is not the angle for any carbon in this molecule. Count the groups around carbon a; a double bond counts once.

q: What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at carbon a in 2-pentyne?
h: A triple bond counts as one group. How many groups surround carbon a?
w: Carbon a has only two groups (the triple bond and one single bond), so they point in opposite directions: 180°, which is why the four carbons around the C≡C are drawn in a straight line. 120° is the angle at a double-bonded carbon.
x: 120° goes with three groups, like a C=C carbon. Carbon a is part of a triple bond, which counts as one group.
109.5° goes with four single bonds. Carbon a has a triple bond and only one other bond.
90° is not the angle for any carbon here. Count the groups around carbon a; the triple bond counts once.

q: Diethyl ether was one of the first surgical anesthetics. What is the approximate C–O–C bond angle at oxygen a?
h: Oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs. Count all four groups, not just the bonds.
w: Oxygen a has two bonds and two lone pairs, four groups arranged roughly tetrahedrally, so the C–O–C angle is about 109.5° (bent; the real value is a bit larger). Choosing 180° counts only the two bonds and ignores the lone pairs.
x: 120° goes with three electron groups. Oxygen a has two bonds plus two lone pairs, so count those too.
180° counts only the two bonds and ignores the two lone pairs on oxygen. Lone pairs push the bonds closer together.
90° is not a normal angle around oxygen. Count all of oxygen's electron groups, bonds and lone pairs.

q: Butanal, a sharp-smelling aldehyde, is drawn below. What are the approximate bond angles around carbons a and b?
h: Carbon a has only single bonds (two to hidden H atoms). Carbon b has a C=O and a hidden H. Count groups on each.
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (two C and two hidden H): 109.5°. Carbon b has three groups (C, =O and a hidden H): 120°. "Both 120°" trusts the 120° corners of the drawing instead of counting groups around each carbon.
x: Carbon a is drawn at a 120° corner, but it has four single bonds (two to hidden H). Count groups instead of trusting the drawing.
Carbon b has a C=O, so it has only three electron groups (C, =O and a hidden H). Four single bonds would be needed for 109.5°.
Carbon a has four single bonds, and carbon b has a double bond, not a triple bond. Count the groups on each.

q: Methamphetamine is shown. What is the approximate C–N–C bond angle at nitrogen a?
h: This nitrogen has two bonds to carbon, one hidden H and one lone pair. How many groups is that?
w: N a has three bonds (two C and one H) plus one lone pair: four groups, pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron, so the angle is about 109.5° (slightly less) and the shape around N is pyramidal. 120° trusts the zig-zag drawing and ignores the hidden H and the lone pair.
x: Trigonal planar trusts the zig-zag drawing. This N also has a hidden H and a lone pair; count every group.
180° would need only two electron groups. N a has two C, one hidden H and a lone pair.
Electron groups spread out in 3-D, not in a flat square. Count the four groups on N, including the lone pair.

q: Toluene is drawn below. What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at ring carbon a?
h: Count the groups around carbon a. Remember the hidden H, and that a double bond counts once.
w: Each benzene-ring carbon has three groups (two ring carbons and one H, with one double bond), so the ring is flat and every angle is 120°, a perfect hexagon. 109.5° would need four single bonds on the carbon.
x: 109.5° would need four single bonds. Ring carbon a has two ring carbons, one hidden H and one double bond: three groups.
180° goes with two electron groups. A benzene ring carbon has more groups than that.
90° would make a square, but a benzene ring is a flat hexagon. Count the three groups around carbon a.

q: In 4-methyl-2-pentyne, which statement about the bond angles at carbons a and b is correct?
c: a is about 109.5° and b is 180°
a is about 120° and b is 180°
a is about 109.5° and b is 120°
h: Carbon a has only single bonds; carbon b is part of the triple bond. Count groups on each.
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (three C plus one hidden H): 109.5°. Carbon b has two groups (the triple bond and one single bond): 180°. Choosing 120° for a trusts how the branch is drawn; it is not a double-bond carbon.
x: Carbon a is drawn with branches at 120°, but it has four single bonds (three C and a hidden H). Count groups, not drawn angles.
Carbon a is not part of the triple bond. It has four single bonds, so it is not linear.
Carbon b is part of the triple bond, so it has only two groups. 120° would need three groups, as at a C=C carbon.

q: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?
h: Every corner and line end is a carbon. Fill in enough hidden H atoms to give each carbon four bonds, then add the masses.
w: Counting every carbon and every hidden H gives C9H8O4: 9(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 4(16.00) = 180.15 g mol⁻¹. 173.10 g mol⁻¹ counts only the H atoms written on O or N and forgets the H atoms hidden on the carbons (the most common mistake); 168.14 g mol⁻¹ misses one carbon (count every corner and line end); 94 g mol⁻¹ adds atomic numbers instead of atomic masses.
x: That total uses only the H atoms written on O or N. Add the hidden H atoms on the carbons too, enough to give each carbon four bonds.
That total is one carbon short. Every corner and line end is a carbon, including ring corners and the ends of short branches.
That is what you get by adding atomic numbers. Use the atomic masses from the table, multiplied by the number of each atom.

q: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?

q: Capsaicin, shown, is the compound that makes chili peppers hot and is used in pain-relief creams. Besides the benzene ring, which functional groups does it contain?
c: an amide, an ether, a phenol and an alkene
an ester, an ether, an alcohol and an alkene
an amide, a ketone, a phenol and an alkyne
an amine, an ether, a phenol and an alkene
h: Look at each heteroatom: a C=O bonded to N is an amide; O between two carbons is an ether; OH on the ring is a phenol.
w: The N–H next to a C=O makes an amide (not an amine or ester); the –OCH3 on the ring is an ether; the –OH on the ring is a phenol; and the C=C in the chain is an alkene. There is no isolated ketone and no triple bond.
x: An ester needs an O next to the C=O, but here the C=O is bonded to N–H. And –OH directly on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol.
The only C=O is bonded to an N, so it is not a ketone. The chain has a C=C double bond, not a triple bond.
An amine has N with no C=O next to it. Here the N–H is bonded directly to the C=O carbon.

q: Veterinarians and emergency physicians use ketamine, drawn here, as an anesthetic. Ignoring the benzene ring, what three functional groups does the drawing contain?
c: a ketone, a secondary (2°) amine and a halogen
an aldehyde, a primary (1°) amine and a halogen
a ketone, an amide and a halogen
an ester, a secondary (2°) amine and an alcohol
h: Where is the C=O? Count the carbons on the N. Is the Cl on a carbon?
w: The C=O is inside the ring bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone (an aldehyde would need an H on the C=O). The N bonds to two carbons (CH3 and the ring carbon) and is not bonded to the C=O carbon, so it is a 2° amine, not an amide. The Cl on the ring is a halogen (organohalide) group.
x: An aldehyde needs an H on the C=O carbon, but here the C=O is inside the ring, between two carbons. The N also has two carbons on it, not one.
An amide needs N bonded directly to the C=O carbon. Here the N is on a neighboring ring carbon, not on the C=O carbon.
An ester needs an O next to the C=O, and an alcohol needs an –OH. The drawing has neither; Cl and O are the only non-carbon atoms besides N.

q: Four nitrogen- or oxygen-containing compounds are drawn. Pick the one that is an amide.
h: An amide has a nitrogen bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon (C=O).
w: Only the first structure has N bonded to a C=O carbon: it is N-methylpropanamide. The compound with N but no C=O is an amine; the one with –O– next to C=O is an ester; the C=O flanked by two carbons is a ketone.
x: This one has an N but no C=O, so it is an amine.
Here the C=O carbon is bonded to an –O–CH<sub>3</sub>, which makes an ester.
Here the C=O is between two carbons, which makes a ketone. There is no nitrogen.

q: Compounds I and II both have the formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> and the same polar C–Cl bonds. Which statement about their polarity is correct?
c: I is nonpolar because its two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; II is polar.
II is nonpolar because its two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; I is polar.
I and II are equally nonpolar, because they contain exactly the same bonds.
I and II are equally polar, because every C–Cl bond is polar.
h: Bond polarity is not enough: the molecular shape decides whether the bond dipoles add up or cancel.
w: In the trans isomer (I) the two Cl atoms sit on opposite sides of the flat molecule, so the C–Cl dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel: I is nonpolar. In the cis isomer (II) both Cl atoms are on the same side, the dipoles add, and II is polar. Having identical bonds does not make molecules identical in polarity; shape matters.
x: This reverses the two drawings. Look at which one has the two Cl atoms on opposite sides of the C=C and which has them on the same side.
Same bonds do not mean same polarity. Shape decides whether the C–Cl dipoles cancel or add up.
Polar bonds can still cancel if they point in opposite directions. Check whether the two Cl atoms are on the same side or opposite sides.

q: This aldehyde also carries an OH group. Give its IUPAC name.
h: The aldehyde carbon is C1 and sets the name; the OH is a "hydroxy" prefix with its own number.
w: The –CHO carbon must be C1 (an aldehyde is always at the chain end). Counting from it, the OH is on C3: 3-hydroxybutanal. "2-hydroxy" and "4-hydroxy" count from the wrong carbon; "butanone" would need a ketone C=O in the middle of the chain.
x: Count from the –CHO carbon as C1. The –OH is not on the carbon right next to it; one CH<sub>2</sub> lies in between.
The -one ending is for a ketone, with C=O between two carbons. Here the C=O is at the end of the chain with an H: an aldehyde.
This numbers from the wrong end. The –CHO carbon must be C1, so count from the aldehyde end.
